_slice: United States subnational — the state, county and municipal layer, with California and Los Angeles as the worked vertical
_note: Built to correct the largest single distortion in the corpus. Before this slice the United States was 33 reports, of which 28 were federal and 5 institutional — zero state, zero county, zero municipal — against Canada's 41 provincial and 15 municipal. The graph was asserting that Canadian federalism has structure and American federalism does not, which is the opposite of true. The shape follows the Canadian branch deliberately: a federal statistical frame, one worked state, one worked county and city inside it. California and Los Angeles were chosen for documentation quality rather than size — the Board of Equalization writes to all 58 county assessors every December naming the inflation factor, which is as clean a documented dependency as this corpus contains. Two findings worth carrying forward. First, the Medicaid matching rate — the largest federal-to-state transfer mechanism in the country — is computed from BEA state per capita personal income over a Census population denominator, so two statistical series decide how federal health spending divides between fifty states. Second, California's constitutional spending limit on every city and county is a ratio whose numerator is a federal series published in the Survey of Current Business; a national statistical agency sets the growth rate of local government spending authority in a state that did not ask it to.

reports.title: Census of Governments
reports.description: The complete enumeration of every state and local government in the United States, conducted every five years in years ending in 2 and 7 under Title 13 U.S.C. §161. Three components — Organization (the count and classification of counties, municipalities, townships, special districts and school districts), Public Employment and Payroll, and Public Finance. In census years the entire universe of roughly 90,000 local governments plus the 50 states is canvassed; in the four intervening years the Bureau collects from a sample instead, which is why the census functions as the benchmark for the annual series.

release_schedule.rule: Conducted every five years, in years ending in 2 and 7, under Title 13 U.S.C. §161.
release_schedule.note: A year-precision entry, which is the honest width: the cycle year is fixed by statute and the month within it is not.

reports.title: Government Units Survey (Census of Governments: Organization component)
reports.description: The organization component of the Census of Governments, described by the Bureau as "the only source of periodic information that identifies and describes all units of government in the U.S." It collects location, name, legal status and organisational structure for every government, and maintains the Governments Master Address File — the frame from which every other Census public-sector survey draws its sample.

entries.covers: Public Sector: Government Organization data release (annual Government Organization counts/tables, successor to the Sept 24, 2025 release)

release_schedule.note: Census Bureau's official 'Upcoming Releases' calendar (census.gov/data/what-is-data-census-gov/upcoming-releases.html) lists 'Public Sector: Government Organization' scheduled for 9/24/2026 on data.census.gov & API. This is the annual Government Organization data product that GUS feeds; the Census Bureau began publishing these tables annually starting Sept 24, 2025 (per its press release), in addition to maintaining the traditional quinquennial Census of Governments cycle (years ending in '2' and '7' - so the next full Census of Governments: Organization component with Individual State Descriptions Report and Organization Summary Report would be the 2027 cycle, likely released in 2028-2029 based on the 2022 cycle's timing: 2021 GUS collection -> Organization data release Summer 2023 -> Individual State Descriptions Spring 2024). No exact date has been published yet for the full 2027 cycle deliverables.

reports.title: Annual Survey of State Government Finances (ASFIN)
reports.description: Annual revenue by source, expenditure by object and function, indebtedness, and cash and security holdings for state governments, conducted since 1951. Unlike the local-government side of the programme it is a complete enumeration rather than a sample: the technical documentation states the data "are not subject to sampling error because this is a complete enumeration of all 50 State governments." Coverage extends to dependent state entities including state universities, pension systems and insurance trusts. Each state's own accounting records are recoded to a uniform Census classification so that states are comparable despite differing legal structures.

entries.covers: FY2023 state government finance data release
FY2024 state government finance data release

release_schedule.note: Census Bureau has not published a release calendar or stated rule for ASFIN. The two most recent editions were both released in early March: FY2023 data on 2025-03-27 and FY2024 data on 2026-03-05 (press releases titled 'New State Government Finance Data'). An earlier edition (FY2020 data) was released 2021-12-16, showing the exact month has shifted over time, so the March timing should be treated as a recent pattern rather than a fixed rule. Next edition (FY2025 data) is projected for around March 2027 based on this recent pattern; not confirmed by the Bureau.

reports.title: Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates (SAIPE)
reports.description: Annual model-based estimates of median household income and of the number and rate of people in poverty for every state and county, plus school-age (5-17) poverty counts for all 13,000+ school districts. It exists because direct survey estimates for small areas are too imprecise: SAIPE combines direct American Community Survey estimates with regression predictions built from IRS exemption counts, SNAP participation, population estimates, BEA personal income and prior decennial counts, using shrinkage estimation weighted by the reliability of the survey component. It is the operative statistical input to Title I education funding.

release_schedule.note: Census Bureau's SAIPE newsroom updates page states verbatim: 'The 2025 release is planned for December 2026.' No specific day given, only the month. The most recent release (2024 SAIPE estimates) was published January 27, 2026 (https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2024-saipe.html), consistent with SAIPE being an annual release though the exact month has varied across years (Dec 2023, Dec 2024, Jan 2026).

reports.title: Boundary and Annexation Survey (BAS)
reports.description: The annual collection from tribal, state and local governments of "the correct boundary, name, and status information" for legally defined geographic areas — incorporated places, minor civil divisions, counties and equivalents, reservations and trust lands. It is the mechanism by which annexations, incorporations, disincorporations and consolidations enter the Census geographic database, and it is the named source of record for adds and deletes of general-purpose governments in the Governments Master Address File.

entries.covers: 2027 BAS cycle: boundary changes in effect by Jan 1, 2027 reported, with governments' responses due by the Mar 1, 2027 deadline

release_schedule.rule: BAS runs annually: legal boundary changes must be legally in effect on or before January 1 to be reported in the current survey year; the Census Bureau contacts eligible governments in early January to begin the survey; boundary changes returned by March 1 are reflected in that year's American Community Survey and Population Estimates Program data (a secondary May 31 deadline captures changes for next year's BAS materials instead).
release_schedule.note: The 2026 BAS cycle (Jan 1, 2026 effective-date cutoff, Mar 1, 2026 response deadline, delayed start in early Feb 2026) has already concluded as of the 2026-08-11 reference date, so the next occurrence is the following annual cycle. Census has not yet published specific 2027 dates; the Jan 1 cutoff / Mar 1 deadline pattern is the publisher's standing annual rule, applied here to compute the next cycle. releases_per_year=1 is consistent with this being a single annual survey cycle.

reports.title: Personal Income by State (State Personal Income and Employment)
reports.description: BEA's measure of "the income people living in each state and the District of Columbia get from wages, proprietors' income, dividends, interest, rents, and government benefits," on a place-of-residence basis and consistent with the national accounts. Published in total and per capita. The per capita figure is the operative input to the Medicaid matching formula, which is why the population denominator matters: BEA uses the Census Bureau's July 1 midyear estimates.

release_schedule.note: Not independently scheduled — released bundled with the GDP third estimate.

reports.title: Personal Income by County, Metro, and Other Areas
reports.description: Personal income below the state level — counties and county equivalents, metropolitan and micropolitan areas, and BEA economic areas — on the same conceptual basis as the state and national accounts. The estimates are hierarchically constrained rather than freely estimated: "County estimates sum to state totals which, together with the estimate for the District of Columbia, sum to a national total which equals the NIPA estimate." Because county source data are thin, the estimates lean on state unemployment insurance wage records and on Census inputs.

entries.covers: GDP by County and Personal Income by County, 2025

release_schedule.note: BEA's release schedule page lists this as 'GDP by County and Personal Income by County, 2025' scheduled for December 2, 2026 at 8:30 AM. This combined county-level release corresponds to the corpus report 'Personal Income by County, Metro, and Other Areas', which BEA releases annually each December alongside GDP by County.

reports.title: Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (FMAP) — annual Federal Register notice
reports.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Secretary
reports.description: The annual notice announcing each state's Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, the enhanced FMAP for CHIP, and disaster-recovery adjustments for the coming federal fiscal year. Computed under §§1905(b) and 1101(a)(8) of the Social Security Act from state and national average per capita personal income, floored at 50 percent and capped at 83 percent. Governs federal matching for Medicaid, TANF Contingency Funds, Child Support, CCDF and Title IV-E foster care and adoption assistance — the single largest federal-to-state transfer mechanism in the United States.

release_schedule.rule: 42 U.S.C. §1301(a)(8)(B): the Secretary shall promulgate the Federal percentage "between October 1 and November 30 of each year".
release_schedule.note: A statutory window rather than a date, and the schema renders it as one. The window is two months wide, so it is filed at quarter precision — the narrowest band that does not claim a day the statute does not give.

reports.title: Title I, Part A State and Local Educational Agency Allocations
reports.publisher: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Elementary and Secondary Education
reports.description: Annual allocations to states and local educational agencies under the four Title I-A formulas of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act — Basic, Concentration, Targeted, and Education Finance Incentive Grants. Driven by counts of children aged 5 to 17 in families below the poverty level, for counties and school districts.

release_schedule.note: The corpus URL (www2.ed.gov state tables page, which redirects to www.ed.gov's 'President's Budget State Tables' series) is the correct page — it explicitly covers 'Department of Education programs that allocate funds to States or local educational agencies using statutory formulas,' including Title I, Part A. The page itself states: 'Updates to the State tables are posted as a package... Major updates normally are posted for significant milestones in the appropriations process, such as the President's Budget Request and enactment of an appropriation, and when the Department makes awards under certain formula grant programs -- usually in July and October.' This is a real publisher-stated description, but it gives no fixed/computable date. Checking actual file timestamps across the last three editions confirms the timing is not consistent: the FY2023-2025 edition's files were originally posted around October 2024 (per URL path /sites/ed/files/2024-10/...), the FY2024-2026 edition's files carry a last-modified date of 2025-06-13, and the current FY2025-2027 edition's files carry a last-modified date of 2026-04-02 (verified via HTTP HEAD on https://www.ed.gov/media/document/state-tables-state-fy-2025-fy-2027-113554.xlsx and the companion by-program file). That's roughly one edition per year but posted in three different months (Oct, June, April) with no consistent time-of-year, so it does not meet the bar for 'observed-pattern' (consistent time of year) — classified as irregular. No new (FY2026-2028) edition was found as of 2026-08-11; probing plausible filename/date patterns on ed.gov for a next edition returned nothing.

reports.title: Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) Allotments and IMD DSH Limits
reports.description: The Federal Register notice publishing each state's Medicaid DSH allotment — the cap on federal DSH matching — and the Institutions for Mental Diseases DSH limits, determined under §1923(f) of the Social Security Act. Each year's allotment is the prior year's escalated by the change in the CPI-U, with preliminary allotments using an estimated change and final allotments the actual.
reports.cadence_note: Nominally annual, published irregularly in practice — the most recent notice covered four fiscal years at once (FY2020 through FY2023).

release_schedule.note: CMS bundles multiple fiscal years' final and preliminary DSH/IMD-DSH allotment figures into a single Federal Register notice at irregular intervals -- observed notices: 2013-07-26 (FY2012 final/FY2013 preliminary), 2017-11-03 (FY2015 final/FY2017 preliminary), 2019-02-11 (FY2017 final/FY2019 preliminary), 2022-03-16 (FY2018-19 final/FY2020-21 preliminary), 2023-04-14 (FY2020-21 final/FY2022-23 preliminary). Gaps range from ~1 to ~4 years and no notice covering later fiscal years (FY2022+ final or FY2024+ preliminary) could be found as of 2026-08-11, over 3 years since the last notice. Neither the Social Security Act §1923(f) provision nor CMS/Medicaid.gov materials state a fixed publication deadline (e.g., 'by X days before FY start') for these combined notices -- CMS states allotments are calculated 'according to statutory requirements' but the finalization/publication has historically lagged years behind the fiscal year in question, per MACPAC's own analysis of the process. No calendar, stated rule with a computable date, or consistent yearly pattern could be established; this is a genuinely irregular release schedule despite releases_per_year=1 on file.

reports.title: CHIP State Allotments
reports.description: Annual federal allotments of Children's Health Insurance Program funds to states, computed under §2104(m) of the Social Security Act by escalating the prior year's allotment (or the state's prior-year expenditures) by an "allotment increase factor" — the product of a per capita health care growth factor and a state child population growth factor.

release_schedule.rule: 42 CFR 457.609(a)(1): "the national CHIP allotment and State CHIP allotments will be posted in the Medicaid Budget and Expenditure System/State Children's Health Insurance Program Budget and Expenditure System and at Medicaid.gov ... as soon as practicable after the allotments have been determined for each Federal fiscal year."
release_schedule.note: There is a governing regulation (42 CFR 457.609) confirming allotments are determined once per federal fiscal year (consistent with the corpus's releases_per_year=1), but the posting timing is only specified as "as soon as practicable" -- no fixed date or computable next-occurrence. Historical Federal Register 'Final Allotments to States' notices (FY2000: published May 24, 2000; FY2012: published July 24, 2012; FY2013: published July 26, 2013) show no consistent month across years, and the medicaid.gov/chip/financing page itself has not been updated with a new allotments document since FY2012 final/FY2018 preliminary allotments (PDFs dated 2019 upload, content from Dec 2017). Since CHIP funding has since been extended for years at a time by statute (e.g., through FY2029), CMS does not appear to issue a new dated public allotments release on a predictable annual calendar. Could not find any current (2024-2026) dated allotments notice or calendar to support a computable next date.

reports.title: National Health Expenditure Projections
reports.publisher: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Office of the Actuary
reports.description: Ten-year projections of national health spending by payer and by service, produced by the CMS Office of the Actuary. The projected per capita figure is named in statute as one of the two factors escalating every state's CHIP allotment, which makes an actuarial projection a direct determinant of a federal transfer.

release_schedule.note: CMS OACT publishes NHE Projections roughly annually but with no fixed month or stated rule for timing; observed release dates for recent editions have ranged from February to September: 2016-2025 ed. released Feb 15, 2017; 2017-2026 ed. Feb 14, 2018; 2018-2027 ed. Feb 20, 2019; 2021-2030 ed. Mar 28, 2022 (2019/2020 editions were delayed/skipped, likely COVID-related); 2022-2031 ed. Jun 14, 2023; 2023-2032 ed. Jun 12, 2024; 2024-2033 ed. released ~Sep 2025 (Health Affairs DOI 10.1377/hlthaff.2025.00545); 2025-2034 ed. released Jun 24, 2026 (CMS/Fierce Healthcare). Because the month of release has varied by more than half a year across recent cycles, no specific next-occurrence date can be responsibly computed; the next edition (2026-2035) is expected sometime in 2027 but the CMS landing page states only that projections are produced 'annually' without specifying a month.

reports.title: Highway Safety Grant Program Funding Tables (Section 402 apportionments)
reports.description: The annual apportionment of Section 402 State and Community Highway Safety formula funds to the states, District of Columbia, territories and tribes. Under 23 U.S.C. §402(c)(2), 75 percent is apportioned on each state's share of national population as determined by the most recent decennial census, and 25 percent on each state's share of national public road mileage.

release_schedule.note: NHTSA posts one 'Grant Funding Table' (covering Section 402 and 405 apportionments) per federal fiscal year (period 'October 1 to September 30'), but the actual posting date within that fiscal year varies significantly and is not on a fixed calendar or stated rule: the FY2023 table was posted in March 2023 (https://www.nhtsa.gov/sites/nhtsa.gov/files/2023-03/15884-FY%202023%20Grant%20Funding%20Table-tag.pdf), the FY2024 table was dated June 13, 2024 (https://www.nhtsa.gov/sites/nhtsa.gov/files/2024-06/16297-FY%202024%20Grant%20Funding%20Table_061324-v1-tag.pdf), and the FY2025 table was posted in a June 2025 folder (https://www.nhtsa.gov/sites/nhtsa.gov/files/2025-06/fy-2025-grant-funding-table-tag.pdf). An interim FY2022 table was also dated December 15, 2021 and covered only a partial period ('October 1, 2021 to February 18, 2022'), consistent with tables being tied to congressional appropriations action (continuing resolutions and final appropriations acts) rather than a fixed date. Neither 23 U.S.C. 402 nor NHTSA's site states a specific deadline for the Secretary/NHTSA to apportion Section 402 funds each year (unlike the July 31 deadline that applies only to reapportionment of previously-withheld funds). The FY2026 table already exists as of August 2026 (https://www.nhtsa.gov/document/grant-funding-table-fy-2026), so the next edition would be the FY2027 table, but no reliable date can be computed given the observed 3-6 month spread across years.

reports.title: Governor's Budget (California)
reports.description: The Governor's annual proposed budget for the ensuing fiscal year, submitted to the Legislature under Article IV §12 of the California Constitution "within the first 10 days of each calendar year", with itemized statements of recommended expenditures and estimated revenues. Revised each May as the May Revision and enacted as the Budget Act, which the Legislature must pass by midnight on June 15.

release_schedule.rule: Governor's Budget submitted by January 10 each year (CA Constitution Art. IV §12); May Revision by May 14 (Gov. Code §13308).
release_schedule.note: 2026's January 10 and May 14 deadlines have already passed as of this audit — entries project the next full cycle.

reports.title: State of California Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The state's GAAP-basis audited annual financial report — government-wide and fund statements, management discussion, notes and a statistical section — issued under Government Code §12460, which requires a report "prepared strictly in accordance with 'Generally Accepted Accounting Principles'". Issued alongside a separate budgetary-legal basis annual report.

release_schedule.note: California Government Code Section 12460 requires the Controller to compile and publish this report but explicitly leaves timing to the Controller's discretion ('in the time, form, and manner prescribed by him or her') — no statutory deadline exists. There is no published release calendar. Historical release timing (from Independent Auditor's Report dates found in the PDFs on the publisher's site) has been highly irregular relative to fiscal year end (June 30): FY2022 report (FYE 6/30/2022) — auditor's report dated March 8, 2024 (~20 months lag); FY2023 report (FYE 6/30/2023) — auditor's report dated December 5, 2024 (~17 months lag); FY2025 report (FYE 6/30/2025) — auditor's report dated May 5, 2026, transmittal letter May 12, 2026 (~10.5 months lag, described by the Controller's own transmittal letter as 'notably the fastest turnaround for the ACFR in recent years'). These releases span March, December, and May across different years — no consistent time-of-year pattern — so this does not meet the bar for observed-pattern. One report per fiscal year (releases_per_year=1) does appear correct; only the calendar timing within the year is unpredictable. The FY2026 report (FYE 6/30/2026, just ended as of today 2026-08-11) has not yet been posted; based on the improving-but-variable trend, it could plausibly appear anywhere from roughly spring 2027 to a year or more later, but no defensible specific date can be computed.

reports.title: Price Factor and Population Information (Article XIII B appropriations limit factors)
reports.publisher: California Department of Finance, Demographic Research Unit
reports.description: The annual letter transmitting to every California city and county the two factors that adjust the Article XIII B appropriations limit — the "Gann limit". Attachment A gives the price factor, the percentage change in California per capita personal income; Attachment B gives each city's and unincorporated county's population percentage change as of January 1. Revenue and Taxation Code §2227 requires transmission by May 1; the higher population estimate is certified to the State Controller by June 1.

release_schedule.rule: California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 2227: "Such statements shall be transmitted by May 1" — the Department of Finance must transmit its estimate of the percentage change in population (and, in practice, the accompanying price factor for Article XIII B appropriations limit calculations) to local agencies by May 1 each year.

entries.covers: FY 2027-28 price factor and population information (Article XIII B appropriations limit factors)

release_schedule.note: The FY 2026-27 edition was already transmitted via cover letter dated May 1, 2026 (confirmed via a third-party-hosted copy of the DOF letter), so that occurrence is in the past relative to today (2026-08-11); the next occurrence is computed as May 1, 2027. This May 1 deadline is corroborated by an unbroken observed pattern of DOF cover letters dated May 1 in multiple years checked (e.g. May 1, 2003 and May 1, 2026), and by the DOF site's live page currently showing the 'May 2026' edition as current.

reports.title: E-1 and E-5 Population and Housing Estimates for Cities, Counties and the State
reports.publisher: California Department of Finance, Demographic Research Unit
reports.description: California's official January 1 population (E-1) and population-and-housing (E-5) estimates for the state, all 58 counties and every incorporated city, built from housing stock change, occupancy and persons-per-household, and administrative records. These are the statutory population figures for California per capita allocations, and the State Controller uses them to distribute state subventions to cities and counties.

entries.covers: January 1, 2027 E-1/E-5 population and housing estimates

release_schedule.rule: Annually, the Department of Finance shall transmit to each city and each county an estimate of the percentage change in population... Such statements shall be transmitted by May 1. (Cal. Revenue and Taxation Code Section 2227)
release_schedule.note: DOF press releases confirm this statutory May 1 deadline is met in practice: the 2026 E-1/E-5 estimates were released May 1, 2026, and the 2025 estimates were released May 1, 2025. The most recent release (May 1, 2026) has already occurred as of 2026-08-11, so the next expected release is May 1, 2027.

reports.title: Principal Apportionment (Local Control Funding Formula)
reports.description: The certified allocation of state school funding to local educational agencies, dominated by the Local Control Funding Formula, computed from attendance reported by districts and property tax data reported by county auditors. Certified four times a year: Advance by July 20, First Principal Apportionment by February 20, Second Principal Apportionment by June 25, and Annual by the following February 20.

entries.covers: Annual Apportionment for FY 2025-26 (initial AN certification)

release_schedule.rule: The Principal Apportionment consists of four annual certifications: Advance Apportionment certified by July 20 (based on prior-year data, covers state aid payments July-January); First Principal (P-1) Apportionment certified by February 20 (supersedes Advance, covers February-May payments); Second Principal (P-2) Apportionment certified by June 25 (supersedes P-1, provides final June state aid payment); and Annual Apportionment (AN) certified by February 20 of the following year (supersedes P-2, later recertified as AN R1/R2/R3).
release_schedule.note: Confirmed actual FY2025-26 certification dates found on CDE site: Advance certified July 18, 2025; P-1 certified February 18, 2026; P-2 certified June 19, 2026 (all already past relative to today, 2026-08-11). The FY2026-27 Advance Apportionment (nominally due by July 20, 2026) likely already occurred just before today's date but its exact certification date/letter was not directly located on the site, so it is not listed as a future entry. Listed entries are the next future occurrences of each of the four recurring certification types, computed from the stated July 20 / February 20 / June 25 / February 20 rule.

reports.title: Proposition 98 Minimum Funding Guarantee calculation
reports.description: The annual computation of the constitutional minimum funding level for school and community college districts under Article XVI §8 of the California Constitution, identifying which of Test 1, Test 2 or Test 3 operates and the resulting guarantee for the prior, current and budget years. Published inside the Governor's Budget, the May Revision and the enacted budget rather than as a document of its own.

entries.covers: Governor's Budget FY2027-28 - initial Proposition 98 guarantee calculation
May Revision FY2027-28 - updated Proposition 98 guarantee calculation

release_schedule.rule: The Proposition 98 minimum funding guarantee is first calculated in the Governor's Budget, which the Governor must submit to the Legislature on or before January 10 each year (Cal. Constitution Art. IV Sec. 12(a); Gov. Code Sec. 13337); the calculation is then updated in the May Revision, which the Department of Finance releases in mid-May each year (Gov. Code Sec. 13308).

reports.title: Local Tax Distributions by City and County (Bradley-Burns)
reports.publisher: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration
reports.description: The distribution of the Bradley-Burns uniform local sales and use tax and district transactions taxes to cities, counties and districts, paid as two monthly advances plus a quarterly cleanup payment in February, May, August and November, together with the published statistics of amounts distributed by jurisdiction. Advances are computed from the prior year's like quarter; the cleanup reconciles to actual returns.

entries.covers: FY 2024-25 Local Tax Distributions by City and County (Table 21A) data added to the dataset
FY 2025-26 Local Tax Distributions by City and County (Table 21A) data (projected next annual update)

release_schedule.note: This is an ANNUAL dataset, not quarterly. CDTFA's own statistics page classifies it under 'Annual Report Tables: Sales and Use Taxes,' and the underlying OData API (queried directly) shows one fiscal-year record set added per year for 13 straight fiscal years (2012-13 through 2024-25), with the most recent addition (FY2024-25) timestamped LastUpdated=2025-11-24. Fiscal years run July 1-June 30, so a ~5-month lag after fiscal year close (June 30) to publication (~late November) is the observed pattern; the corpus's releases_per_year=4 appears to describe a different, related CDTFA quarterly Bradley-Burns disbursement product, not this specific Table 21A dataset. No explicit publisher-stated rule (e.g. 'published X months after fiscal year end') was found, so this is classified as observed-pattern rather than stated-rule.

reports.title: Cities Annual Report / Cities Financial Transactions Report
reports.description: The Controller's compiled annual report of the financial transactions of California cities, with companion reports for counties and special districts, built from Financial Transactions Reports each local agency must file under Government Code §53891. Government Code §12463 requires the compilation to "encompass appropriations limits and the total annual appropriations subject to limitation" — which makes this the document where every city's Gann limit is recorded. The California analogue of a municipal financial information return.

entries.covers: FY 2025-26 Cities Financial Transactions Report filings (deadline ~7 months after June 30, 2026 fiscal year-end)

release_schedule.rule: California Government Code Section 53891(a): the officer of each local agency (city) having charge of financial records must furnish to the State Controller a report of all financial transactions of the agency during the preceding fiscal year, "within seven months after the close of each fiscal year, or within such further time as the Controller may prescribe" (whichever is later). The Controller compiles these city filings into the Cities Annual Report / Cities Financial Transactions Report dataset published via the ByTheNumbers portal.
release_schedule.note: This is the statutory deadline by which individual California cities must submit their financial transactions data to the State Controller's Office; the SCO then compiles/publishes the aggregated Cities Annual Report / Cities Financial Transactions Report and ByTheNumbers database on a rolling basis as filings arrive (no single fixed publication date found). Could not directly access the publisher's own landing page (https://www.sco.ca.gov/ard_locrep_cities.html) or its PDF alert letters, which returned 403/Cloudflare-challenge errors during this research session, so no dated release calendar could be confirmed directly from the publisher; this finding relies on the governing statute plus corroborating secondary references to the same filing deadline.

reports.title: Letter To Assessors: Annual Proposition 13 Inflation Factor
reports.publisher: California State Board of Equalization, Property Tax Department
reports.description: The annual letter instructing all 58 county assessors what inflation factor to apply to factored base year values on the coming roll. Revenue and Taxation Code §51 compounds base year values by this factor, which Article XIII A §2(b) of the California Constitution caps at 2 percent. One short letter, issued days before the lien date, that sets the growth rate of the property tax base for the whole state.

release_schedule.note: The BOE Property Tax Department issues a Letter To Assessors each year announcing the annual inflation factor under Revenue & Taxation Code Section 51 (base year values compounded by the CCPI percentage change, capped at 2%). There is no published release calendar and no statutory deadline for the letter's issuance date itself (only the underlying CPI computation method is statutorily fixed); observed issuance dates cluster in late December to mid-January, immediately before/around the January 1 lien date for the following fiscal year. The most recent letter, LTA 2026/002 (Jan 13, 2026), already covers FY2026-27 inflation factor (1.02); the next letter (for FY2027-28) is expected around December 2026-January 2027 based on this pattern, but no confirmed date exists yet as of 2026-08-11.

reports.title: California Consumer Price Index
reports.publisher: California Department of Industrial Relations, Division of Labor Statistics and Research
reports.description: The California-specific consumer price index maintained by the Division of Labor Statistics and Research. It is a distinct series from the national CPI-U, and it is the index Revenue and Taxation Code §51(a)(1)(C) names as the source of the Proposition 13 inflation factor — so California property assessment tracks a state index, not a federal one.
reports.cadence_note: Filed as monthly on the strength of the published series; the exact release cycle was not confirmed from a DIR methodology page this pass. The statutory read is October to October regardless of how often it appears.

release_schedule.rule: Published on even-numbered months only (six times a year), roughly seven weeks after the reference month, per the California DIR's own published schedule.
release_schedule.note: Corrects releases_per_year, previously recorded as 12 — DIR's own site (landing page, a 2019 methodology notice, and a Dec 2025 notice) states publication on even-numbered months only. Also depends specifically on BLS *regional* CPI releases (LA, SF, San Diego, Riverside metro indexes), not the national bls-cpi headline release — DIR skipped October 2025 entirely when the federal shutdown delayed BLS regional data. Candidate edge, not yet added: ca-dir-ccpi depends on BLS regional CPI, needs a proper basis before minting.

reports.title: Los Angeles County Annual Assessment Roll
reports.publisher: Los Angeles County Office of the Assessor
reports.description: The annual roll of assessed value for all locally assessed real and personal property in Los Angeles County, valued as of the 12:01 a.m. January 1 lien date, comprising the regular secured and unsecured roll and the supplemental roll. Countywide assessed valuation was approximately $2.123 trillion for FY2024-25. The roll must be completed by July 1 and is then delivered to the County Auditor-Controller.

release_schedule.rule: BOE Publication 29 important dates: "January 1 — Lien date for all property"; "July 1 — Deadline for county assessor to complete local assessment roll".
release_schedule.note: The deadline is a day, so this is day precision — but note it is a deadline rather than a publication date, which is the one case where an exact date can still be later than the truth.

entries.covers: roll for the January 1, 2027 lien date

reports.title: Los Angeles County Property Tax Apportionment and Allocation Reports
reports.description: The published apportionment and tax-rate report series dividing the 1 percent general levy and voter-approved debt levies among more than 1,300 local agencies — the County, cities, school districts, special districts and redevelopment successor agencies. Includes the AB 8 apportionment factor file, modified ATI ratios, assessed-valuation reports and tax-rate reports. The American counterpart of a provincial equalized assessment and requisition apportionment.

entries.covers: FY 2024-2025 Apportionment and Allocation Reports (bulk upload)
FY 2025-2026 Apportionment and Allocation Reports (bulk upload)
FY 2026-2027 Apportionment and Allocation Reports (next expected bulk release)

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar or statutory deadline was found on the Auditor-Controller's site for this report family. Examining the upload directory timestamps on the Property Tax Report Central page (auditor.lacounty.gov/property-tax-report-central/) shows a consistent annual pattern: for each fiscal year (which begins July 1), the bulk of that year's apportionment/allocation/valuation/rate reports are uploaded in a cluster spanning August through October (e.g. 2017/08-09, 2018/08-09, 2019/08-10, 2020/09-11, 2021/08-10, 2022/09-10, 2023/08-10, 2024/08-11, 2025/09-11). For FY2026-2027 (current fiscal year as of 2026-08-11), a smaller initial batch was already uploaded in 2026/02 and 2026/07, with the main annual cluster expected to continue through roughly October 2026 based on the historical pattern.

reports.title: Los Angeles County Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The audited annual financial report of the County and its component districts, issued under California Government Code §25253 and prepared under GAAP for governmental entities. Its property tax note records the 1 percent levy limit, the county's 13,197 tax rate areas and the January 1 lien date, and its statistical section carries a ten-year assessed value schedule.

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar and no statutory deadline found (Cal. Gov. Code Section 25253, which the report cites as its governing authority, requires an annual report but specifies no publication deadline). Observed pattern from actual PDF publication dates on the Auditor-Controller site: FY 2023-2024 ACFR was published January 2025 (file path /wp-content/uploads/2025/01/...) and FY 2024-2025 ACFR was published January 2026 (file path /wp-content/uploads/2026/01/...), i.e. ACFRs are consistently released in January, roughly 6-7 months after the June 30 fiscal year end. Next edition (FY 2025-2026, year end June 30 2026) is projected for January 2027 by this pattern.

reports.title: City of Los Angeles Revenue Outlook
reports.publisher: City of Los Angeles, City Administrative Officer
reports.description: The annual supplement to the Proposed Budget forecasting each General Fund revenue source. The property tax chapter — roughly a third of General Fund revenue — builds its forecast from County Assessor assessed-value growth for the City, County Auditor-Controller payment estimates, the Proposition 13 cap and Proposition 8 decline-in-value adjustments.

release_schedule.note: The CAO's Revenue Outlook is released each year as a supplement to the Mayor's Proposed Budget. Editions checked (FY2020-21, FY2021-22, FY2022-23, FY2023-24, FY2026-27) are all dated/titled 'April [year]' on their cover page. This aligns with LA City Charter Sec. 312, which requires the Mayor to submit the Proposed Budget to Council on or before April 20 each year, though no publisher statement gives a specific day for the Revenue Outlook itself, so it is treated as an observed pattern rather than a stated rule. Next edition (FY2027-28) is projected for April 2027.

reports.title: City of Los Angeles Proposed Budget
reports.publisher: City of Los Angeles, Mayor and City Administrative Officer
reports.description: The Mayor's proposed annual budget for the fiscal year beginning July 1, presented to Council in April, of which the Revenue Outlook is the revenue-estimate supplement.

release_schedule.rule: On or before April 20 of each year, the Mayor shall submit to the Council a budget for the next ensuing fiscal year (LA City Charter Sec. 312, Mayor's Proposed Budget).
release_schedule.note: Confirmed by actual practice: Mayor Bass released the FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget on April 20, 2026, exactly matching the Charter's April 20 deadline. Since April 20, 2026 has already passed relative to today (2026-08-11), the next occurrence is April 20, 2027.

dependencies.basis: The annual survey is a sample drawn against, and benchmarked to, the quinquennial census universe rather than an independent collection. NCES's documentation of the Census government finance series states directly that "The sample of local governments is drawn from the periodic Census of Governments (which is conducted in years ending in '2' and '7')." The Census Bureau's own programme FAQ confirms the same structure from the other side: "Every five years (years ending in '2' and '7') we conduct a census, in which we attempt to collect financial data from all local governments," and "For the four years between our censuses, we collect data from a sample of governments."

The Government Units Survey FAQ states that "The GUS provides critical information on organizational structure that we need to maintain the universe frame of governments. Public sector surveys that the Census Bureau conducts use the frame to draw their samples." The GUS about page adds that the Bureau uses the resulting Governments Master Address File "as a benchmark for all our non-census year samples." The annual finance survey is one of those non-census-year public sector surveys, so its sample frame is the file GUS maintains.
dependencies.evidence_quote: The GUS provides critical information on organizational structure that we need to maintain the universe frame of governments. Public sector surveys that the Census Bureau conducts use the frame to draw their samples.

Decisions to add or delete county, municipal, or township governments to the GMAF are made on the basis of information obtained through the annual Boundary and Annexation Survey, which the Census Bureau's Geography Division conducts."

dependencies.basis: The State Government Finances methodology page directs users to the Census of Governments for the definitional and organisational basis of the survey: "See Chapter 1 of the Government Finance and Employment Classification Manual and the 2007 Census of Governments" for information on government definitions and organization. The survey recodes each state's own administrative accounting records into the classification framework established for the census.
dependencies.evidence_quote: See Chapter 1 of the Government Finance and Employment Classification Manual and the 2007 Census of Governments

dependencies.basis: The ACS is the dependent variable in every SAIPE county model. The county-level estimation documentation specifies the modelled quantity as "the log of the total number of people in poverty in each county as measured by the ACS", and for children "the log of the number of related children in poverty ages 5 to 17 in each county as measured by the ACS". The methodology overview records the switchover: "The most significant change was between 2004 and 2005, when SAIPE began using data from the American Community Survey, rather than from the Annual Social and Economic Supplement to the Current Population Survey."

The county model includes as regression predictors "the log of the estimated total resident population as of July 1" and "the log of the estimated resident population under age 18 as of July 1", which are the Bureau's postcensal estimates. Population also enters as the denominator converting modelled poverty counts to poverty rates.

reference_period.stated_as: Estimated resident population as of July 1 enters the model as a predictor and as the rate denominator.

dependencies.basis: The official thresholds define both the concept SAIPE estimates and one of its regression predictors. The county model uses "the log of the number of tax return exemptions (all ages) on returns whose adjusted gross income falls below the official poverty threshold", and correspondingly the child-exemption equivalent. The IRS administrative predictor is thus constructed by applying the official poverty thresholds to tax return income.

Decennial poverty and income counts enter the county models as regression predictors — the documentation names "the log of the Census 2000 estimate of the total number of people in poverty", the related-children equivalent, and "the log of the Census 2000 estimate of county median household income" — and the estimation strategy page lists "decennial census estimates" among the programme's input sources. Caveat carried forward from research: the published methodology names Census 2000 specifically, so the vintage should be re-checked against the current estimate year.

The SAIPE county median household income model uses two BEA-derived predictors: "the log of the proportion of the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) estimate of total personal income derived from government transfers" and "the log of the growth of BEA total personal income from 1999 through the target year". These are county-level covariates in a county model, so the relevant BEA product is the local area series.

BEA's Local Area Personal Income and Employment: Concepts and Methods states: "In computing annual per capita personal income for states and counties, BEA uses the Census Bureau's annual midyear (July 1) population estimates." Per capita personal income is a headline output of the local area series, so the Census estimates are a direct computational input.

reference_period.stated_as: Census Bureau annual midyear (July 1) population estimates, used as the per capita denominator.

dependencies.basis: BEA's local area methodology states: "Estimates of rental income of persons are based on place of residence data from the American Community Survey (ACS)." Rental income of persons is a component of the property income portion of personal income, so ACS is a named source for a component of the county estimates.
dependencies.evidence_quote: Estimates of rental income of persons are based on place of residence data from the American Community Survey (ACS).

dependencies.basis: The county estimates are constrained to the state accounts rather than estimated freely: "County estimates sum to state totals which, together with the estimate for the District of Columbia, sum to a national total which equals the NIPA estimate." The county figures are therefore an allocation of independently estimated state totals.

BEA's State Personal Income and Employment: Concepts and Methods carries the same statement for states: "In computing annual per capita personal income for states and counties, BEA uses the Census Bureau's annual midyear (July 1) population estimates." Per capita personal income by state is the figure the Medicaid matching formula reads, so this denominator propagates into every state's FMAP.

reference_period.stated_as: Census Bureau annual midyear (July 1) population estimates, used as the per capita denominator.

dependencies.basis: The State Personal Income methodology states that "Estimates of rental income of persons are based on place of residence data from the American Community Survey (ACS)." ACS is a named source for the rental income component of state personal income.
dependencies.evidence_quote: Estimates of rental income of persons are based on place of residence data from the American Community Survey (ACS).

The Census Bureau names the product and the allocation in its own release: "SAIPE statistics are used to allocate funding under Title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act... The U.S. Department of Education plans to use the 2021 estimates to calculate fiscal year 2023 allocations for Title I and several other federal education programs." The Department of Education's annual memorandum to State Title I Directors transmits the SAIPE tables directly and links census.gov/programs-surveys/saipe.html.

dependencies.evidence_quote: SAIPE statistics are used to allocate funding under Title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act... The U.S. Department of Education plans to use the 2021 estimates to calculate fiscal year 2023 allocations for Title I and several other federal education programs.

The CMS notice implementing it states that allotments are determined "using the most recent available estimates of or actual medical assistance expenditures, including DSH expenditures and the most recent available CPI-U data for the FY in accordance with the methodology prescribed in the statute."

dependencies.basis: 23 U.S.C. §402(c)(2)(B)(i) provides that "75 percent shall be apportioned to each State based on the ratio that, as determined by the most recent decennial census — (aa) the population of the State; bears to (bb) the total population of all States", with the remaining 25 percent on public road mileage. The mileage half is certified by each Governor rather than taken from a published statistical series, so only the population half is an edge here.

reference_period.stated_as: "the most recent decennial census" — a read that stays fixed between censuses, so the apportionment share moves once a decade however often the funds are apportioned.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §7901(a) defines the price factor as a ratio whose denominator is DOF's own population estimate: California personal income "divided by the civilian population of the state on January 1 of the next calendar year, as estimated by the Department of Finance". Section 7901(b) defines the local change in population as "the percentage change in population between January 1 of the next calendar year and January 1 of the calendar year in question, as estimated by the Department of Finance."

reference_period.stated_as: Civilian population as of January 1, compared with January 1 of the prior year.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §7901(a): "'Change in California per capita personal income' means the number resulting when the quotient of the California personal income, as published by the United States Department of Commerce in the Survey of Current Business for the fourth quarter of a calendar year divided by the civilian population of the state on January 1 of the next calendar year, as estimated by the Department of Finance, is divided by the similarly determined quotient for the next prior year." The Gann price factor is therefore a federal BEA series over a state population denominator — a constitutional spending limit on every Californian city and county driven by a national statistical agency.

reference_period.stated_as: California personal income for the fourth quarter of the calendar year, as published in the Survey of Current Business.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §12463(a) requires the Controller to compile and publish the financial transactions reports of counties, cities and special districts, and provides that those reports "shall encompass appropriations limits and the total annual appropriations subject to limitation". The appropriations limit each city reports is the Article XIII B limit computed from the DOF price and population factors; DOF states it "will certify the higher [population] estimate to the State Controller by June 1".

The State Controller's City Financial Transactions Report Instructions state: "The FTR requirements conform to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) as prescribed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB)." The instructions cite Government Code §12463 et seq. as the authority for the report and §53891(a) as the requirement that cities furnish it.

Government Code §12460 requires the Controller to "issue a comprehensive annual financial report prepared strictly in accordance with 'Generally Accepted Accounting Principles'". The report states that it "meets the requirements of Government Code section 12460 for an annual report prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles", and the auditor's opinion is rendered on that basis — which for a state government means the standards set by GASB.

Government Code §12460 requires the Controller to submit an annual report to the Governor containing "a statement of the funds of the state, its revenues, and the public expenditures" for the preceding fiscal year. The budgetary-legal basis annual report issued under the same section accounts for prior year adjustments, fund balances, encumbrances, revenues and expenditures on a basis aligned with the Governor's Budget and the Budget Act.

Article XVI §8(b)(1) of the California Constitution sets the Test 1 guarantee as "the amount which, as a percentage of General Fund revenues which may be appropriated pursuant to Article XIII B, equals the percentage of General Fund revenues appropriated for school districts and community college districts, respectively, in fiscal year 1986-87." The 2026-27 Governor's Budget applies this to the Department's own General Fund revenue forecast: "The Guarantee continues to be in a Test 1 for 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27. This means that the funding level of the Guarantee is equal to roughly 40 percent of General Fund revenues, plus local property tax revenues."

Article XVI §8(b)(2)-(3) makes the guarantee turn on the same per capita personal income figure that drives the Gann limit: Test 3 applies instead of Test 2 when the change in California per capita personal income exceeds the change in per capita General Fund revenues plus one-half of one percent, in which case prior-year allocations are increased by per capita General Fund revenue growth plus 0.5 percent. The "change in California per capita personal income" is the figure defined by Government Code §7901(a) and published annually by the Department of Finance as the Article XIII B price factor.

Education Code §42238.02 reduces a district's Local Control Funding Formula entitlement by "the property tax revenue received pursuant to Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 75) and Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 95) of Part 0.5 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code" — the supplemental roll and the AB 8 property tax apportionment each county auditor computes from the county assessment roll. The Department states the apportionment uses "pupil attendance, tax, and other data" reported by local educational agencies, special education local plan areas and "county auditors". So a rise in Los Angeles assessed value mechanically reduces the state aid the district receives.

reference_period.stated_as: County tax data are submitted three times a year — P-1 taxes by November 15, P-2 taxes in mid-April, and prior-year annual taxes by August 15 — against a roll valued as of the January 1 lien date.

The enclosure notes the increase "is limited to 2 percent pursuant to California Constitution, article XIII A, section 2(b)".

dependencies.basis: The Letter To Assessors quotes the statutory source: "Section 51(a)(1)(C) provides that for any assessment year commencing on or after January 1, 1998, the inflation factor shall be the percentage change, rounded to the nearest one-thousandth of 1 percent, from October of the prior fiscal year to October of the current fiscal year in the California Consumer Price Index (CCPI) for all items, as determined by the California Department of Industrial Relations." It then applies it: "Information from the Department of Industrial Relations shows that the CCPI increased from 335.150 in October 2023 to 343.575 in October 2024 ... an increase of 2.514 percent", capped at 2 percent.

The total Fiscal Year (FY) 2024-2025 assessed valuation of the County approximated $2.123 trillion." It adds that the levy "is limited to one percent (1%) of full cash value and is distributed in accordance with statutory formulae", across 13,197 tax rate areas.

It also records the timing problem candidly: "No preliminary estimate for Countywide growth in 2026 assessed valuations is available from the County Assessor, which would otherwise serve as the basis for City 2026-27 estimated property tax growth. The Assessor will release its assessment roll forecast in May."

It also notes that the "County Auditor-Controller determines each local jurisdiction's proportionate share of the administrative costs" charged against the City's property tax.

The Revenue Outlook identifies itself in its own title block as "a Supplement to the 2026-27 Proposed Budget", published by the City Administrative Officer. It is the revenue-estimate volume on which the Proposed Budget's revenue assumptions rest, published alongside it in April.

_dropped.why: The Department of Education memorandum does describe the ACS as an input to the counts it uses, but only by way of describing the SAIPE model that produces them. The path is already in the graph as ed-title-i-a-allocations -> uscensus-saipe -> uscensus-acs, and asserting the two-hop as an edge as well would double-count the ACS in the authority calculation. Same reasoning applies to the decennial census and population estimates named in that sentence.

Education Code 42238.02 defines the LCFF base grant cost-of-living adjustment by reference to "the percentage change in the annual average value of the Implicit Price Deflator for State and Local Government Purchases of Goods and Services for the United States", for the 12-month period ending in the third quarter of the prior fiscal year, read as of a fixed May 10 date. Well evidenced and worth having. Not minted because the exact published BEA table for that specific deflator was not confirmed this pass, and inventing a URL for it would be worse than the missing edge. A federal price index setting a Californian school funding rate is a good node once someone pins the table down.

The Revenue Outlook does reason about the Proposition 13 inflation cap — "Growth in this category is capped at two percent by Proposition 13" — but it forecasts from "the western region consumer price index", not the California CPI that Revenue and Taxation Code 51(a)(1)(C) actually prescribes and that the Board of Equalization letter applies. So the document evidences the City modelling the mechanism with a proxy of its own choosing, not the City reading the Board letter. Filed here rather than asserted, and it is not evidence for a bls-cpi edge either.

Almost certainly real — LCFF is the district's principal revenue source. The district's budget pages are JavaScript-rendered and a direct fetch returns a 4.5 KB shell with none of the text, so nothing could be quoted. Re-run with a rendering browser against budget.lausd.org; the candidate pages were identified during research.

LCFF is funded partly from local property tax apportioned by the county auditor, with state aid backfilling the difference, and the county apportionment pages name schools among the recipients. No LAUSD or county document was found stating that the district budget reads the auditor apportionment. Same rendering problem as above.

The two are plainly the same collection instrument split into two published products, and the state survey is described as a supplement to the combined programme. No document states a directional data dependency, and "supplement" is ambiguous about which way it would run. Treated as sibling products of one collection.

The Z.1 state and local government tables are near-certainly built on Census government finance data, and the introductory text references "detailed annual survey data ... from the Census Bureau" for that sector, but it does not name the survey and could plausibly mean the Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions. The per-table source notes in the Financial Accounts Guide would settle it.

The Census classification recodes financial reports that are themselves prepared under GASB, but the Census classification is deliberately independent of GAAP fund accounting, so the honest characterisation may be non-dependence rather than an uncited dependence. The Government Finance and Employment Classification Manual would settle it; the Census PDF path is robots-blocked from this environment.

The E-1 release says the estimates are "benchmarked to the 2020 decennial census" and elsewhere mentions "Census Bureau county proportions", but the decennial census is a different product from the Population Estimates Program and no DOF methodology document naming which Census series is read could be found.

The other 25 percent of the Section 402 apportionment runs on public road mileage which 23 U.S.C. 402(c)(2)(B)(ii) requires to be "certified by the Governor of the State" and approved by the Secretary. A state certification to a federal agency is not a published release and cannot be a node.

_dropped.edge: highway trust fund apportionment -> any statistical series
_dropped.why: A negative finding, and a useful one. Federal highway apportionment under 23 U.S.C. 104(c) reads no statistical series at all: each state's share is "the proportion that (I) the amount of apportionments that the State received for fiscal year 2021 bears to (II) the amount of those apportionments received by all States for that fiscal year". No population, VMT or lane-mile series enters it — the formula is frozen against a base year. Worth recording because the assumption that a big federal transfer must read a statistic is exactly the plausible-sounding link this project exists to exclude.

42 U.S.C. 5306(b) names the CDBG formula variables — population, extent of poverty, housing overcrowding, age of housing, growth lag — but names no data source for any of them, and 24 CFR 570.4 defers entirely to the statute. HUD research publications describe successive decennial and ACS vintages being used in practice, but descriptive research is not a document establishing the dependency. A HUD Federal Register notice or formula methodology document would settle it.

42 U.S.C. 1397dd(b) does name "the 3 most recent March supplements to the Current Population Survey", but that provision governs the pre-2009 allotment formula, not the current section 2104(m) formula. It would be accurate only as a historical edge with an end date, which the model does not carry.

MOVED 2026-08-31 (second independent audit, finding F-05; Thomas's ruling: naming the agency is not naming the artefact): the cited Federal Register notice names the Department of Commerce and 'average income per person in each state' but never BEA or the State Personal Income series. Find the document that names the release itself before re-minting. Original relationship_type: calculated_from. Original basis: "The notice states that "The Secretary calculates the percentages, using formulas set out in sections 1905(b) and 1101(a)(8), and calculations from the Department of Commerce of average income per person in each state and for the United States." 42 U.S.C. §1396d(b) supplies the formula: the FMAP is "100 per centum less the State percentage; and the State percentage shall be that percentage which bears the same ratio to 45 per centum as the square of the per capita income of such State bears to the square of the per capita income of the continental United States", floored at 50 and capped at 83 percent. Caveat: the notice names only "the Department of Commerce"; the identification of BEA as the publishing bureau comes from CRS R43847, which records that "In its FY2025 FMAP calculations, HHS used state per capita personal income data for 2020, 2021, and 2022 that became available from the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in September 2023.""
